title: Katharina von Bora
hookLine: a nun who escaped, tradition says, in a herring cart, married Luther, and ran a brewery, farm and household

cards: Behind a convent wall, in the days before Easter, a group of nuns have been reading pamphlets smuggled in from Wittenberg, and they've decided to leave. Leaving is dangerous.
A merchant who brings goods to the convent agrees to help. One night his covered cart rolls away loaded with empty barrels, barrels that once held herring, tradition says.
Tucked among them, hardly breathing, are the nuns. The cart makes it out. Among the women who climb down at the other end, smelling of fish, is Katharina von Bora.

teach.h: FROM CONVENT TO NO ONE'S HOUSE.
teach.b: Katharina had been placed in a convent as a girl. Now she was out, with no money and no family able to take her in, and the reformers tried to find husbands for the women who had left.
For Katharina, a match was tried and fell through.
Then, the story goes, she let it be known she would marry Luther, or one other man, and no one else. Luther was surprised, and then he did it.
They moved into his old monastery building in Wittenberg, and she turned it into a household.

She brewed beer. She kept a farm, cows and pigs, a garden, an orchard and a fishpond. She fed students who boarded with them, and refugees, and a stream of guests who came to argue theology at her table.
She managed the money, which was not Luther's gift. She nursed the sick, and she raised their children. Luther's letters to her are full of teasing affection.

He calls her my lord Katie, putting the word for a lord or master in front of her name. He calls her a rich woman, a doctor, a preacher, a brewer. In his will he left everything to her, which surprised people at the time.
Proverbs has a poem for a woman like this, the capable wife. In the King James Bible: "She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness."
Catholic and Lutheran readers tell her story differently. For Catholics, leaving a convent broke solemn vows. For the reformers, marriage was a holy calling too.
Either way, a movement runs on someone who keeps the house standing.

how: Lutheran churches remember Katharina von Bora, and some honor her in their calendars of commemoration; her household is often held up in Protestant teaching as a picture of the pastor's family and home.

games.q: you're Katharina, out of the convent with no money. the matches others arrange keep falling through. what do you do?
o: name the man you'd actually marry.
games.why: the story goes that she let it be known she'd marry Luther, or one other man, and no one else. Luther was surprised, and then he married her.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose work keeps your life running and mostly goes unseen: someone who cooks, schedules, cleans, remembers birthdays, pays the bills. Think of one specific thing they did this week.
If you pray, give thanks for them by name; if you don't, simply hold that one thing with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Katharina. The nun who escaped in a wagon of barrels, married Luther, and ran the brewery, farm and household at the heart of the Wittenberg reform.

orig.note: German: 'lord Katie', Luther's teasing, respectful name for his wife in his letters.

carryVoice: Your line: my lord katie. Luther's teasing names were love in plain words. Day eight hundred fifty-six, complete.
